The projection calls for a .216 average and .644 OPS over a full season—a bench player or fourth outfielder line—and while his speed (24 SB projected) offers some thrift value, the core batting risk is severe. Medium confidence given the Statcast data is current and the decline is documented.

656811_hitter.text: Ryan O'Hearn is a league-average power bat with modest walk rates and a contact profile that generates hard contact without significant barrels. His xwOBA (.321, 50th percentile) and xBA (.262, 71st percentile) sit right at the middle of the league, supported by 89.5 mph exit velo (54th) and 43.8% hard-hit rate (62nd), but a meager 5.7% barrel rate (27th) constrains his power ceiling. The main risk is a 33.4% chase rate (29th percentile) paired with a 7.5% walk rate (31st), leaving him dependent on strong contact to generate value—and his Statcast profile suggests that contact alone won't carry a 32-year-old DH who offers minimal speed or defense. Medium confidence given that his Statcast metrics and projection align, but his contact-only profile at age 32 leaves limited room for growth or injury recovery.

656849_pitcher.text: David Peterson is a soft-stuff starter operating in the lower-velocity, lower-spin tier—his fastball sits 92.3 mph with 2159 rpm spin (both 17th percentile)—and relies on modest whiff rates (22.2%, 27th percentile) and command to survive. His Statcast profile shows a 4.84 xERA and .340 xwOBA (both 22nd percentile), and his 8–1 HLD projection with a 4.9 ERA reflects a pitcher who can fill innings but lacks the strikeout or stuff profile to dominate. The primary risk is that weak fastball velocity and spin leave no margin for command mistakes, and his 9.4% walk rate (36th percentile) suggests he's already living on the edge; a modest uptick in free passes or hard contact could push results sharply negative. Medium confidence given the thin separation between his true-talent ERA and his projection floor.

656876_pitcher.text: Rasmussen is a command-and-contact-suppression pitcher who beats hitters without needing to miss a ton of bats — and the Statcast profile backs that up cleanly. His 4.5% BB% sits in the 98th percentile, his xwOBA of .271 and xERA of 2.99 both land in the mid-to-upper 80s percentile-wise, and a 32.6% hard-hit rate in the 85th percentile tells you hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The whiff rate (24.9%, 49th percentile) is the one honest limitation — he's not a swing-and-miss guy, so his margin for error depends on keeping the ball out of the barrel and the walks near zero, which he's done. ValuCast projects 177.1 IP, a 3.01 ERA, and a 1.02 WHIP, though the medium confidence tag reflects the real question here: at 30 with a Tommy John history, the health outlook is the outcome.

656941_hitter.text: Schwarber is one of the most dangerous power threats in baseball — a true 50-homer type who obliterates contact when he finds the ball, and the Statcast profile backs every bit of that reputation. His 20.0% Barrel % sits at the 98th percentile, exit velo at 93.3 mph checks in 94th, and his xSLG of .542 ranks 96th — the contact quality is genuinely elite. The catch, and it's a real one, is that 34.6% Whiff % (6th percentile) and 33.9% K% (1st percentile) — the strikeouts aren't a quirk, they're the tax on everything else, and a cold stretch can look ugly fast. What saves it is a 14.2% BB% (93rd percentile) that keeps his .362 OBP honest and his .904 OPS projection very reachable; ValuCast sees 690 PA, 50 home runs, and 101 RBI out of him this season in Philadelphia.

657041_hitter.text: Lane Thomas is a chase-happy, weak-contact outfielder whose Statcast profile (47th percentile xwOBA, 31st percentile xBA, 4.5% barrel rate) reveals a player unable to square the ball consistently despite elite plate discipline—he walks at 93rd percentile rates but chases 95th percentile often, producing a 19.2% whiff rate. His ValuCast projection of .225/.322/.349 OPS (.688) reflects that disconnect: a 30-year-old generating soft contact (87.2 mph exit velo, 19th percentile) on a below-average power profile who will survive on speed (92nd percentile sprint speed, 9 SB) and restraint but not production. Medium confidence given the gap between his selectivity and his ability to execute at the point of contact.

657277_pitcher.text: Logan Webb is a contact manager, not a strikeout pitcher, and his Statcast profile says exactly that — a 33.6% chase rate (79th percentile) and 5.4% barrel rate (79th percentile) doing the heavy lifting where a 20.5% whiff rate (15th percentile) and 92.5 mph fastball (19th percentile) never will. The walk rate of 6.1% (83rd percentile) is real and keeps him functional despite the soft stuff; he just needs hitters to beat themselves, and enough of them do. ValuCast projects 182.2 IP with a 3.25 ERA and 1.15 WHIP, which tracks — a 3.59 xERA at 66th percentile suggests the run prevention is legitimate, not a sequencing mirage. The ceiling here is a durable mid-rotation anchor who wins ugly; the floor is what happens when a command-and-contact formula meets a lineup with plate discipline.

657746_pitcher.text: Joe Ryan is a strike-thrower who gets outs with command and deception rather than pure stuff — his BB% sits at 5.5% (90th percentile) and he's punching out 28.2% of hitters (86th percentile), but that 93.4 mph fastball and a barrel rate sitting in the 13th percentile tell you there isn't much margin for error when his location slips. The Statcast profile is pretty honest about the tradeoff: his xERA of 3.19 and .280 xwOBA both land in the 81st percentile, legitimate mid-rotation quality, but the hard-hit and exit-velocity numbers in the 20th-to-29th percentile range mean the contact he does allow tends to be loud. ValuCast's current projection has him at a 3.62 ERA over 175.1 innings with 200 strikeouts — a slight ERA-over-xERA gap that reflects the real-world risk of a guy whose margin for error against good fastball hitters is thinner than the strikeout rate implies. He's a real starter, not a mirage, but the carrying skill is the walk rate, and the real flaw is that when he misses, hitters can square him up.

657757_hitter.text: Sheets produces hard contact at an above-average rate and draws walks at a 68th-percentile clip, yielding a 61st-percentile xwOBA of .334 that substantially exceeds his projected batting line. His projected .236 AVG reflects a persistent gap between contact quality and hit rate—a 44th-percentile xBA—driven by a 21.1% whiff rate that ranks in the 68th percentile for swing-and-miss. The floor is a sub-.240 hitter with modest run production despite solid power; the ceiling is closer to a .250 mark with 22 home runs if hit sequencing tightens. Medium confidence given the disconnect between batted-ball value and surface average, and his role as a DH limits positional flexibility.

660271_two_way.text: Ohtani is the only player in baseball you have to scout twice — and both reads come back elite. On the hitting side, the contact quality is almost absurd: .416 xwOBA, 93.8 mph average exit velocity, and a 16.6% barrel rate all sit at 96th percentile or better, and a 15.4% walk rate rounds out a profile that makes .399 OBP look like a floor, not a ceiling. The one honest wrinkle is a 28.3% whiff rate — that's 31st percentile — but when you're barreling the ball at this rate and taking walks at that clip, pitchers are stuck choosing their poison. On the mound, a 98.0 mph fastball, 2485 rpm spin, and 30.9% whiff rate combine for a 2.68 xERA that would anchor a rotation; ValuCast projects him to .286/.399/.552 with 39 home runs as a DH, and the Statcast profile says that's not optimistic.

660670_hitter.text: Ronald Acuña is a walk machine who barrels the ball — the Statcast profile makes that unmistakable. His 14.8% BB% sits in the 94th percentile, his barrel rate (13.1%) is 82nd, and his xwOBA of .378 is 93rd, so the underlying contact quality is genuinely elite even if the 29.3% whiff rate (25th percentile) keeps the batting average ordinary. The one real concern is sprint speed at the 50th percentile — for a player whose stolen-base value has always been tied to elite athleticism, that's a number worth watching as he works back from the ACL. ValuCast's projection (.263/.379/.446, 18 HR, 28 SB in 505 PA) reflects a good-not-peak Acuña, which feels right given the medium confidence and the sprint speed reading; the plate discipline and power contact are fully there, the question is whether the legs come all the way back.

660821_hitter.text: Sánchez generates solid contact quality—elite exit velo (81st percentile), hard-hit rate (80th), and expected slugging (.457, 76th percentile)—but discipline is his ceiling. He draws walks at just 4.3% (5th percentile) and chases at 39.7% (7th percentile), which drags his projection to .264/.316/.431 and limits his run production despite above-average bat speed. The gap between his Statcast skill (.335 xwOBA, 62nd percentile) and his walk rate suggests a player who swings early at pitches others take, leaving value on the table; his modest speed (26th percentile) won't make up for it. Medium confidence reflects the tension between his power tools and his self-inflicted strikeout and walk profile.

661388_hitter.text: William Contreras is one of the cleaner hitters in the National League — a catcher who makes consistent hard contact and almost never strikes out. His 13.2% K rate and 19.0% whiff rate both sit in the 89th and 80th percentiles respectively, and his xBA of .285 (89th percentile) tells you the .286 projection isn't a fluke or a lucky BABIP story — he's genuinely squaring the ball up. The xSLG of .466 (80th percentile) running ahead of his projected .432 SLG suggests there's a little more thump in the bat than the counting stats will show, and ValuCast's projection of 19 HR with a .362 OBP over 645 PA reflects a dependable everyday presence, not a boom-or-bust gamble. The one real ceiling limiter here isn't the bat — it's the legs; a sprint speed of 25.4 ft/s puts him in the 11th percentile, so the floor on his value is tied almost entirely to what he gives you behind the plate.

661395_pitcher.text: Jhoan Duran is one of the most dominant relievers in baseball right now, and the Statcast profile isn't subtle about it — a 40.0% strikeout rate and 40.6% whiff rate both sitting at the very top of the league, paired with a .231 xwOBA and 2.17 xERA that are each in the 99th percentile. The one genuine wrinkle is contact quality when hitters do make contact: a 48.3% hard-hit rate and 92.1 mph average exit velocity are both in the basement, which is the real tension in his profile — he misses a ton of bats, but the ones he doesn't miss tend to sting. ValuCast's projection sees through the noise, projecting a 2.11 ERA with 84 strikeouts over roughly 61 innings and 36 saves for Philadelphia, a workload that reflects closer-level trust. At 28, with 100.2 mph fastball velocity in the 99th percentile, the question isn't whether he's elite — it's whether that hard-hit suppression holds, and right now everything else in his profile is too loud to bet against him.

662139_hitter.text: Varsho is a light-contact outfielder whose pitch-recognition and swing mechanics leave him chasing at rates well above league average, which depresses his ability to generate hard contact and barrel the ball. His xwOBA (35th percentile) and average exit velo (8th percentile) signal a player stuck in the bottom third of the big-league power tier; the projection of .243/.315/.424 tracks with that reality. The athleticism (47th percentile sprint speed, strong fielding) and fringe walk rate (9.1%) offer modest everyday value, but the chase rate (36%, 17th percentile) and whiff rate (67th percentile) are the central issue—he swings at pitches others let go, and misses often when he does. Medium confidence here reflects a full Statcast sample, but the profile is clear: a fourth-outfielder type without room for margin.

662253_pitcher.text: Muñoz is one of the nastiest strikeout arms in the game right now — a 98th-percentile fastball at 99.1 mph paired with a 99th-percentile whiff rate of 41.2% and a 97th-percentile chase rate of 37.5% is a legitimately elite combination, and his 35.6% strikeout rate backs all of it up. The problem is the 9.8% walk rate sitting at just the 31st percentile — he misses bats at a historic clip but doesn't always know where it's going, and that's why his xERA (3.86) and xwOBA (.306) land in the middling 57th and 58th percentile range despite the gaudy swing-and-miss numbers. ValuCast projects 28 saves, a 3.84 ERA, and 85 strikeouts across roughly 59 innings, which tracks as a legitimate closer role if the command holds. The walk rate is the whole ballgame here — when he locates, he's untouchable; when he doesn't, the damage compounds fast.

663436_pitcher.text: Davis Martin is a command-and-contact-management pitcher who lives by keeping hitters out of the zone — his 33.9% Chase % and 6.3% BB% are genuinely elite, and that combination is the whole game for him. The Statcast profile tells the story plainly: the strikeout and whiff numbers are solid but unspectacular (23.8% K%, 26.9% Whiff%), while the hard-hit exposure is a real concern — 45.3% Hard-Hit% is among the worst in the league, and 89.9 mph average exit velo doesn't leave much margin for error when contact gets made. ValuCast projects him at a 3.52 ERA over 170.8 innings with 13 wins and 17 quality starts, but the xERA sitting at 3.86 suggests some fortune is baked into that number. He's a back-of-rotation arm who needs his chase rate to stay elite every single outing, because when hitters do square him up, they're doing damage.

663460_pitcher.text: Bubic projects as a back-end starter or multi-inning reliever with strikeout leverage but material walk risk. His K% sits at the 64th percentile (24.6%), but the 12.6% BB% (11th percentile) and resulting 4.46 xERA (33rd percentile) reveal a pitcher who doesn't command the zone well enough to sustain run prevention despite decent stuff—his fastball sits at 91.8 mph with elite spin (75th percentile, 2398 rpm) but generates limited exit velo damage. The core problem is discipline: he can miss bats, but too many free passes and mediocre barrel prevention will keep him from posting front-line numbers. Medium confidence reflects his ability to thread the needle as a useful depth arm, but his ceiling is capped by the walk rate.

663538_hitter.text: Nico Hoerner is a contact-first middle infielder who survives — and occasionally thrives — almost entirely on bat-to-ball skill and speed, because he's not hitting the ball hard enough to punish anyone. The Statcast profile tells the whole story: 10.8% whiff rate and 7.1% K% are both elite, but 85.5 mph average exit velocity and a 1.0% barrel rate are bottom-of-the-league-level, which is exactly why his xwOBA sits at .323 (50th percentile) despite an xBA of .287 (90th percentile) — he makes contact, it just doesn't go anywhere. The carrying skill is plate coverage and footspeed (28.4 ft/s, 79th percentile), which together manufacture a .258/.328/.358 projection over 687 PA with 23 steals; the real flaw is that the profile has essentially no power ceiling, and if his speed fades, there's very little offensive floor left. He's a useful big-league regular right now, especially with 98th-percentile fielding, but the projection is a 2B starter you don't pay up for.

663554_pitcher.text: Casey Mize is a command-and-contact pitcher who beats hitters with precision, not power — and right now, it's working at an elite level. His xwOBA of .263 and xERA of 2.81 both sit in the 92nd percentile, built on a 5.5% walk rate (90th percentile) and a 29.2% whiff rate that generates genuine swing-and-miss without needing to overpower anyone. The one thing to watch: his 29.4% chase rate ranks in just the 40th percentile, meaning when hitters discipline themselves and stay in the zone, they get decent contact opportunities — which is why the 93.5 mph fastball at the 32nd percentile isn't a footnote, it's the ceiling question. ValuCast projects a 3.27 ERA over 136.5 innings at medium confidence, and the Statcast profile earns that number — the risk is what happens to a strike-thrower with below-average velocity if the whiff rate normalizes.

663556_pitcher.text: McClanahan is a fastball-first starter coming back into focus after injury — the 95.6 mph heater sits in the 69th percentile for velocity, and the 27.1% whiff rate and 31.1% chase rate tell you the stuff still plays. The problem is contact quality: when hitters do connect, they hit it hard — 41.8% hard-hit rate and a 9.6% barrel rate land in the 28th and 23rd percentiles respectively, which is why the xERA sits at 4.31 despite the swing-and-miss numbers holding up. ValuCast projects a 3.50 ERA over roughly 148 innings, but with medium confidence — the gap between what he misses and what he surrenders is the whole story here, and until that contact profile tightens, he's pitching with less margin than his strikeout stuff suggests he should have.

663586_hitter.text: Austin Riley generates above-average exit velocity (78th percentile) and hard-contact rate (69th percentile), yet his swing-and-miss profile is one of the league's worst — a 32.4% whiff rate at the 11th percentile paired with a 29% strikeout rate that's in the bottom quartile. The gap between his power stuff (xSLG .381, 36th percentile) and his actual batting average (.229 projection) reflects a hitter who can't consistently make contact; his xBA sits at the 7th percentile despite above-average hard-hit metrics. ValuCast projects 20 home runs and a .687 OPS over 638 plate appearances, but the contact issues are the ceiling — Riley has the bat speed to generate power, but the swing-and-miss and chase rate (32.5%, 35th percentile) will keep him from a higher offensive floor.

663616_hitter.text: Trevor Larnach projects as a league-average contact hitter with discipline who doesn't generate enough hard contact to fully capitalize on his quality at-bats. His xwOBA sits at the 62nd percentile and his 11.8% walk rate ranks 76th, but his average exit velo of 86.5 mph (13th percentile) and 6.5% barrel rate (33rd percentile) cap his power and slugging ceiling—reflected in a .42 projected SLG and modest 11 home runs over 461 plate appearances. The main risk is that his batting profile depends entirely on stay-in-zone contact and disciplined pitch selection, leaving little margin for error if either dimension slips. Medium confidence given the thin offensive ceiling and marginal power generation at age 29.

663656_hitter.text: Kyle Tucker is a walk machine who doesn't hit the ball hard enough to fully cash in on it. His 12.4% BB% sits in the 84th percentile and his 25.1% chase rate is genuinely elite — the discipline is real — but a 5.8% barrel rate (28th percentile) and 89.1 mph average exit velocity (45th percentile) mean the contact quality just isn't backing it up, and that xSLG of .378 in the 33rd percentile is the honest verdict on his power. The projection — .247/.347/.417, 19 HR over 642 PA — reflects exactly that tension: enough on-base skill to be useful, not enough thump to be the middle-of-the-order force he once looked like in Houston. The one thing that decides his value right now is whether the exit velocity recovers; the eye is fine, the bat speed apparently isn't.

663728_hitter.text: Cal Raleigh is a power-over-contact catcher operating at the extremes: elite walk rate (11.9%, 79th percentile) and contact avoidance (31.4% K, 9th percentile whiff rate) define him, but he's buried by a 1st-percentile xBA (.179) that reflects a swing-and-miss profile that generates barrels (70th percentile) without consistent bat-to-ball results. ValuCast projects .194 AVG with 25 home runs over 517 plate appearances—a near-platoon power bat who punches out too much to drive meaningful run value from the catcher position. Medium confidence reflects the tension between his measurable discipline and his inability to make regular contact; the offensive ceiling hinges on whether the contact floor can rise even modestly.

663757_hitter.text: Grisham's Statcast profile is a quality contact hitter with above-average power and plate discipline—xwOBA in the 82nd percentile, hard-hit rate in the 75th, and walk rate at 93rd—but his actual .228 AVG projection reflects a significant translation gap between exit velo and balls in play. The 19 home runs and .338 OBP carry real value in a projected 536 PA, yet the xBA at just 62nd percentile signals persistent weakness at turning quality contact into hits; strikeout rate (15.9%) is well-controlled, but sprint speed (34th percentile) limits recovery through the basepaths. Medium confidence reflects a player whose tools read better than his results, a pattern that has held despite solid underlying skills.

664023_hitter.text: Ian Happ is a power-over-contact hitter with elite bat quality but a strikeout problem that suppresses his floor: his Statcast metrics show a 56th-percentile xwOBA and 63rd-percentile xSLG, driven by a 87th-percentile barrel rate and 66th-percentile exit velo, yet he whiffs at 31.9% and strikes out at 31.9%—both well below league average. His projection of .230 AVG, .338 OBP, and 28 HR over a full 664 PA reflects that tension: he will hit home runs and walk at an 88th-percentile rate (13% BB%), but batting average will lag behind his underlying quality. High confidence in this profile.

664040_hitter.text: Brandon Lowe is a pure power bat who earns his keep with his bat and almost nothing else — the Statcast profile makes that separation brutally clear. His contact skills are a real problem: 34.8% whiff rate and 26.2% K% both sit in the bottom quarter of the league, and a 33.6% chase rate that ranks 27th percentile tells you pitchers have found a comfortable place to attack him. But when he does connect, it matters — 13.0% barrel rate, 46.2% hard-hit rate, and a .468 xSLG all cluster in the upper tier, which is why ValuCast's projection still gets him to 33 home runs over 614 PA with a .792 OPS. The one thing that decides his value is whether the strikeouts are tolerable given the thump, and at this power level, for a second baseman posting 97th percentile fielding, the answer is probably yes.

664285_pitcher.text: Framber Valdez is a contact-inducing starter running below-average strikeout rates and whiff rates whose command strength keeps him functional: 18.5% K% and 21.0% whiff%, both in the 26th percentile, but 8.2% BB% (54th percentile) and a .321 xwOBA (43rd percentile) that reflect his ability to avoid hard contact despite modest fastball velocity at 95.3 mph. The central risk is that his strikeout floor—158 K over 187 innings in projection—limits margin for error; even light-touch contact pitchers lose leverage if they can't miss bats. ValuCast projects a 3.85 ERA and 1.32 WHIP over a full season's work, reflecting a durable back-end starter profile with high confidence.

664761_hitter.text: Alec Bohm is a collision hitter who can't stay on the ball—high chase and whiff rates (80th and 88th percentiles respectively) are dragging down already modest contact quality, and his xwOBA sits at just the 16th percentile despite league-average exit velo. The projection shows .241/.297/.433, a line that reflects his core problem: he's making too much hard contact relative to actual barrels (4.5%, 19th percentile) and his strikeout rate (14.4%, 85th percentile) is eating into the run production he needs to justify the corner infield spot. Medium confidence given the year-to-year volatility in his approach and the thin gap between his Statcast profile and projection outcomes.

664983_hitter.text: Jake McCarthy is a burner who puts the ball in play and lets his legs do the talking — 99th percentile sprint speed at 29.9 ft/s is the engine that drives everything, and the 17.6% K% (70th percentile) tells you he makes enough contact to weaponize it. The problem is he doesn't hit the ball hard at all: 85.1 mph average exit velo and 25.1% hard-hit rate both sit at the 4th percentile, which is why his xwOBA checks in at .306 (33rd percentile) despite a respectable xBA of .263. ValuCast projects a .286/.334/.451 line with 23 steals over 479 PA, which reads as a useful fourth outfielder who steals bases and avoids strikeouts — the floor is real, but the ceiling is capped by contact quality that ranks near the bottom of the league.

665019_hitter.text: Clemens generates loud contact — his 92.3 mph exit velo (91st percentile) and 12.5% barrel rate (80th) project genuine power, and his xwOBA of .333 (61st percentile) validates solid quality of contact. But a .236 AVG on a .301 OBP projection reveals the core problem: a 6.8% walk rate (21st percentile) and middling plate discipline (31.6% chase rate, 25.4% whiff) leave him reliant on hard contact without the selectivity to build counting stats. Confidence is moderate given Clemens is a depth option whose power tools are real but whose inability to reach base frequently enough will cap his fantasy and roster utility.

665152_pitcher.text: Dean Kremer operates as a back-end starter with below-average velocity and spin—his fastball sits 93.7 mph (30th percentile) with 2273 rpm (43rd percentile)—leaving him dependent on command and sequencing to generate outs. His ValuCast projection shows a 4.38 ERA across 73 innings with a 1.27 WHIP, reflecting a pitcher who will give you length but limited margin for error; strikeout rate figures to be modest relative to his innings pitched. The core risk is that fastball profile offers little room for mistake-making against major-league hitters. Medium confidence given the modest arsenal and the full-season projection window.

665161_hitter.text: Jeremy Peña is a light-contact hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills (96th percentile xBA) and outstanding athleticism (92nd percentile sprint speed) who generates weak contact at the point of impact. His xwOBA of .345 (73rd percentile) and xBA profile suggest a .278 AVG hitter, but his 87.2 mph average exit velo (20th percentile) and 4.0% barrel rate (15th percentile) constrain his power ceiling—the projection of 15 home runs reflects that gap. The weak contact limits his ceiling despite strong process metrics; his value sits in the high-speed, low-power shortstop profile at age 28 rather than any gap-closing breakthrough. Medium confidence given the disconnect between hit quality and batted-ball authority hasn't narrowed over his career arc.

665487_hitter.text: Tatis is a plus athlete with genuine bat-to-ball feel — his xBA sits at .292 (92nd percentile) and he's making hard contact at a 54.1% rate (98th percentile), so the .280/.351/.424 ValuCast projection is not a reach, it may even be conservative if he stays healthy. The one real flaw in the profile is contact quality at contact: a 28.9% whiff rate (27th percentile) caps his ceiling, because all that exit velo and speed can only do so much when he's missing pitches he should be hitting. The 34 projected steals are real — 28.9 ft/s sprint speed puts him in the 90th percentile — so the counting-stat floor is cushioned by legs even in a down power year. He's a five-category contributor, not a superstar rediscovery story, and ValuCast is projecting him accordingly.

665489_hitter.text: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is one of the hardest hitters to strike out in baseball — 10.8% K rate puts him in the 96th percentile — and that contact quality is genuine, with a 93rd-percentile xBA of .294 that says he earns his average, not just runs into it. The disconnect to watch is the barrel rate: at 6.7% (35th percentile), the raw power hasn't been translating into over-the-fence damage at the rate you'd expect, and ValuCast's projection reflects that tension — .279/.363/.418 with 17 home runs across a full 660 PA is a productive first baseman, not the force majeure his talent suggests he could be. The 88th-percentile fielding and a 10.2% walk rate keep the floor comfortable, but until the barrel number catches up to the contact, this profile is more on-base machine than middle-of-the-order thumper.

665742_hitter.text: Juan Soto is the most complete hitter in baseball right now, and the Statcast card makes the case without needing much help. His xwOBA (.427) and xSLG (.606) both land at the 100th percentile — meaning the underlying contact quality is as good as it gets — and he pairs that with a 20.0% chase rate that sits in the 96th percentile, so pitchers genuinely cannot expand the zone on him. The 15.8% walk rate (97th percentile) and 12.3% strikeout rate (93rd percentile) together produce a plate discipline profile that almost doesn't exist at his power level. ValuCast projects a .288/.414/.550 line with 35 home runs in 605 PA; the one honest footnote is that sprint speed (25.7 ft/s, 16th percentile) means the 15 projected steals are a stretch and his defensive ceiling in the outfield is limited, but no one is paying Soto to run.

665833_hitter.text: Oneil Cruz is one of the most violent contact-makers in baseball — 96.0 mph average exit velocity and 59.2% hard-hit rate both sit at the 100th percentile — but he gives a huge chunk of it back at the plate because he simply can't make consistent contact, whiffing at 37.8% (2nd percentile) with a 34.6% K% that ranks dead last. The .358 xwOBA (81st percentile) and .490 xSLG (86th percentile) tell you the raw damage is real when he connects, and the ValuCast projection of 23 HR and 33 SB in 497 PA reflects a player who can hurt you in multiple ways. The strikeout rate is the whole story — if it doesn't come down, he'll always be a boom-or-bust guy who leaves production on the table, and the 10.6% BB% suggests the zone awareness is there enough to keep him from being unplayable. Medium confidence here is honest: the power and speed are elite, the bat-to-ball is a genuine problem, and the gap between those two facts is what Cruz's career hinges on.

665862_hitter.text: Jazz Chisholm is a speed-and-pop profile held hostage by contact problems that the Statcast card makes impossible to ignore — a 32.3% whiff rate sitting in the 11th percentile, with an xBA of .208 at the 8th. The exit velocity is real (90.3 mph, 69th percentile) and the walk rate is quietly good at 10.6%, but when he misses this often, those tools don't convert: his xwOBA sits at .295, 22nd percentile, and ValuCast's full-season projection reflects exactly that tension — .227/.310/.412 with 25 home runs and 40 stolen bases across 604 PA. The stolen bases are genuine; the 81st-percentile sprint speed backs that up, and the 98th-percentile OAA suggests elite defensive value wherever you play him. Contact is the one thing that decides this, and right now the bat-to-ball hasn't caught up to the rest of the package.
